analysis.one_liner: Makes companies that spill oil pay the full cleanup and compensate fishing, property, and subsistence losses, backed by industry fees.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a Senate vote: after one day of subcommittee hearings it sat in the Environment and Public Works Committee until the Congress ended, though a separate oil pollution liability law was enacted in August 1990.
analysis.plain_summary: Written in the months after the Exxon Valdez disaster, this bill would have replaced a patchwork of four overlapping federal oil spill laws with one system: the company responsible for a spill must pay for the cleanup and compensate people and governments harmed — fishermen, coastal property owners, state and tribal governments — with costs above the company's liability limit paid from a fund financed by fees on oil. Tanker and facility owners would have to prove they can cover their maximum liability before using U.S. ports, and vessels without certification could be turned away. The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, whose environmental subcommittee held one day of hearings in July 1989; it never reached the Senate floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents and owners of damaged property, commercial fishermen and others whose livelihoods depend on natural resources (the bill lets anyone deriving at least 25% of earnings from natural-resource activities recover lost profits), state and local governments (lost property taxes and royalties), and Indian tribes (loss of subsistence use is a specifically recoverable damage). Federal and state taxpayers also benefit, because the responsible party — not the public — is the primary payer, and the backstop fund is financed by fees on oil rather than general tax revenue.

how_it_helps.text: Makes the party responsible for a spill strictly, jointly, and severally liable for cleanup costs and damages, shifting the burden from taxpayers and victims to the spiller.

Creates a fund, financed by fees on oil and able to borrow up to $500 million from the Treasury, to pay claims that exceed the responsible party's liability or that the party cannot pay, and lets state governors and tribal officials draw on it immediately for emergency response.

Requires vessels over 300 gross tons and offshore facilities to prove financial responsibility up to their liability limits, and lets the government deny U.S. port entry to tankers that cannot certify coverage.
Allows victims to sue in federal court under state law for economic damages exceeding liability limits, and preserves state funds and penalties on top of the federal system.

analysis.who_pays: Oil companies, tanker and vessel owners, offshore facility operators, and their insurers and guarantors, who face strict liability, mandatory financial-resurance requirements, per-barrel civil penalties, and fees that finance the spill fund. A portion of the fund's costs, being fees on oil, would likely be passed to consumers at the pump.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil companies, tanker owners, and insurers

drawbacks.text: Liability is capped at $78 million for a tanker and $75 million for a facility (with exceptions for willful misconduct or failure to cooperate), well below the cost of a catastrophe like the Exxon Valdez spill, leaving victims dependent on the fund above those limits.
The fund itself is capped at $500 million per incident, and because it is financed by fees on oil, ordinary consumers share part of the cost of compensation.

The bill channels claims into federal court (state courts are barred), confines review of the Secretary's regulations to the D.C. Circuit, and caps the penalty for destroying irreplaceable natural resources at $10 million — all limits an honest supporter would acknowledge favor industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core design — polluter pays, with an industry-financed backstop fund and proof-of-coverage requirements — is the framework that eventually became law, and it was a genuine shift of catastrophic-spill costs off taxpayers and victims. But the caps matter: at $78 million for a tanker, the bill would not have forced a Valdez-scale spiller to bear anything near the full cost, and the $500 million fund ceiling funded partly by oil fees means the public backstops the difference. Victims also lose access to state courts. On balance the bill helps ordinary people more than it costs them, but it is not the unlimited-liability approach the post-Valdez moment made politically available.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, got one day of subcommittee hearings in July 1989, and never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Sen. John Chafee introduced the bill on May 18, 1989, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
The subcommittee on environmental protection held hearings on July 21, 1989, printed as S.Hrg. 101-272; no markup, floor vote, or further action followed.
The bill drew no cosponsors and never received a vote in either chamber.

After the Exxon Valdez spill, multiple competing oil spill bills were pending in the 101st Congress; a comprehensive Oil Pollution Act was enacted in August 1990, superseding this bill's subject matter.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and shipping interests benefited for another year from the weaker, fragmented pre-1990 liability rules this bill would have replaced, though the delay was temporary — Congress enacted a comprehensive oil pollution liability law in August 1990.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and shipping interests, until OPA 90

for.name: Sen. John H. Chafee
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-RI); introduced the bill by request
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill, which was read twice and referred to committee.

for.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Subcommittee on Environmental Protection
for.what_they_did: Held hearings on the bill on July 21, 1989, printed as S.Hrg. 101-272.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and Senate leadership
against.role: Committee of referral and floor schedule
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill to the floor; after the July 1989 hearings no markup or vote ever occurred, and the bill died at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Oil and shipping industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed strict, joint-and-several liability and sharply expanded spill liability during the post-Valdez debate, favoring capped liability.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the partisan split on this bill is unknown; the sponsor was a Republican and the bill was introduced by request, with no recorded opposition in the congressional record.

industries.note: They would bear strict joint-and-several liability for spill cleanup and damages, mandatory financial-responsibility certification, per-barrel penalties, and fees funding the trust fund. Liability caps of $78-75 million and the $500 million fund ceiling, however, keep their worst-case exposure well below catastrophic-spill costs.

Guarantors and insurers can be sued directly by claimants up to policy limits, raising their exposure, but the mandatory financial-responsibility requirement forces vessel and facility owners to buy their coverage.

industries.industry: Commercial fishing and coastal tourism businesses
industries.note: The bill makes lost profits and earning capacity from damaged natural resources explicitly recoverable for those deriving at least a quarter of their earnings from such activities, giving an industry hit hardest by spills a direct claim against spiller and fund.
